Business infrastructure works the same way. As companies modernize, [DevOps services](https://www.orangemantra.com/services/devops-solutions/) have become that backbone: invisible when it works, costly when it’s ignored. 

So what does DevOps infrastructure management cost in 2026, and how might that number shift over the next year or two? I will not include the cost of DevOps consulting here, as I will cover that in my upcoming blog.  

Worldwide IT spending is projected to hit [$6.31 trillion in 2026](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-04-22-gartner-forecasts-worldwide-it-spending-to-grow-13-point-5-percent-in-2026-totaling-6-point-31-trillion-dollars), up 13.5% from last year, with data center and cloud infrastructure investment leading that growth, according to Gartner.

Before pricing anything out, it helps to know what falls under the DevOps umbrella. It’s not just one tool or one bill. A DevOps setup includes several moving parts working together, and each one contributes to your overall DevOps development cost.

* **CI/CD tooling automates** building, testing, and deploying code, so releases happen faster and with fewer manual errors.
* **Cloud hosting and compute** cover the servers and networking your applications actually run on.
* **Monitoring and observability tools** track performance and errors so problems get caught before users notice them.
* **Security and compliance tooling** handles vulnerability scanning and audit requirements, especially important for regulated industries.
* **Container orchestration** platforms like Kubernetes manage how applications scale and stay resilient across environments.

And underneath all of it is people and team time, the engineers and [DevOps specialists](https://www.orangemantra.com/services/hire-devops-engineer/) who configure, maintain, and troubleshoot these systems daily.

How much does it cost to make an app? The average cost of developing an app ranges from US $60,000 to $250,000.

If you’ve ever pitched a mobile product idea to a CTO or a CFO, you’ve heard the question already: “It’s just an app. How much could it really cost to make?” The honest answer is that the number moves a lot, and most of that spread comes down to choices you make about the project.

That range is the going market rate. For focused, well-scoped healthcare builds, smart use of AI in our development process can bring the cost in from around $25,000, with a typical AI-accelerated build landing near $49,000, under the $60,000 industry floor above. Deeply custom and enterprise builds still run higher, which the rest of this guide breaks down.

As a healthcare app development agency, cost estimation is all we can give you up front for a custom web or mobile product. The final price tag comes down to the number and complexity of screens, the platform choice (multiplatform = more effort), ongoing maintenance, and the QA program your app actually needs.

At Topflight Apps, we break the cost to build an app into four buckets:

* Design: branding, animations, [UX/UI design](https://topflightapps.com/ideas/7-step-ultimate-guide-to-mobile-app-design/), design system foundations
* Technical build: API and platform integrations, business logic, infrastructure, third-party SDK setup
* QA: test plans, manual exploratory testing, automation, regression cycles before release
* Maintenance: server costs, bug fixing, OS upgrades, security patching

Policy as code (PaC) takes the same principles that transformed infrastructure management, declarative definitions, version control, testing, and automation, and applies them to organizational rules and guardrails.

Policies are written in code-like languages, stored in Git, and enforced automatically in pipelines or runtime environments. This includes both “decision engines” that evaluate policies at runtime and “static analyzers” that scan IaC before deployment.

In this article, we’ll explore some of the most widely used policy-as-code tools and platforms from general-purpose engines, cloud-native frameworks, and provider-specific solutions.

## What is policy as code?

Policy as code (PaC) is the practice of writing governance, security, and compliance rules as machine-readable files that tools can automatically evaluate and enforce. It replaces static policy documents with automated checks in CI/CD, infrastructure provisioning, and runtime.

![a diagram showing how policy as code works](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fspacelift.io%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2023%2F03%2Fpolicy-as-code.png&w=3840&q=75)

Common uses include blocking public S3 buckets, enforcing required tags, validating Kubernetes resources on admission, or failing Terraform plans that violate controls. You’ll often combine multiple layers: static checks in PRs, admission policies in clusters, and org-level guardrails in your cloud accounts.

**Read more:** [What is Policy as Code (PaC) & How Do You Implement It?](https://spacelift.io/blog/what-is-policy-as-code)

Spacelift is the publisher of this article. We’ve included ourselves so you can compare directly, but treat this entry as a vendor perspective, not an independent ranking.

## Popular tools used for policy as code

Policy-as-code tools let teams define rules declaratively, integrate them into CI/CD pipelines, and audit changes through version control. They help enforce consistent security, compliance, and operational policies across environments. 

We will review the tools in the following categories:

| Misconfig scanning | Pre-commit / PR | IaC files before they reach main | Checkov |
| Terraform / IaC enforcement | IaC pipeline (plan / apply) | The proposed change against org rules | Spacelift, HashiCorp Sentinel |

| App authorization | Runtime authz | Who can do what inside your app | AWS Cedar |
| General policy engine | Cross-layer engine | The decision engine the others build on | Open Policy Agent |

A typical setup looks like Checkov in CI, Spacelift gating the apply, Gatekeeper at admission, and SCPs as the last-line guardrail. Each layer catches the things the layer below it can’t see. The question isn’t “which one of these tools do I pick” but “where do I have a gap”.

Every ADAS sensor fusion algorithm, every over-the-air update pathway, every battery management module introduces requirements that trace across electrical, mechanical, and software domains at the same time. According to McKinsey, the software content in vehicles is growing at about 15% annually, and that growth multiplies the number of cross-domain requirements that teams need to track, verify, and maintain by an order of magnitude.

That complexity hits hardest in compliance. ISO 26262 demands traceability from vehicle-level safety goals down through technical safety requirements, hardware and software specifications, and verification evidence. Platforms with continuous, automated traceability catch change impacts that manual processes miss.
* **ISO 26262, ASPICE, and ISO/SAE 21434 each impose distinct traceability requirements.** A tool that covers functional safety well may not address cybersecurity or process maturity assessments. Evaluate platforms against all the standards your organization needs to satisfy.
* **Supply chain collaboration is an architectural requirement.** OEMs and Tier 1 suppliers co-develop systems that span organizational boundaries. ReqIF interchange and secure cloud-based collaboration aren't nice-to-have features; they're operational necessities for multi-company development programs.
* **The gap between ALM tools and requirements management platforms matters in automotive.** ALM platforms built for software development may handle ASPICE process areas well but lack depth in hardware safety analysis and system-level hazard decomposition.

**End-to-end traceability across domains.** Automotive systems span software, electronics, mechanical components, and more and more, AI/ML models. A requirements tool needs to trace relationships from vehicle-level safety goals through system architecture, component specifications, and verification results across all of these domains.
